Benign Degeneracy for First-Order Methods in Exact Boolean Moment–SOS Relaxations

Shucheng Kang

School of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Harvard University

`skang1@g.harvard.edu`

**Abstract**

Pseudo-Boolean optimization--minimizing a polynomial over \(\{\pm 1\}^n\)--includes MAX- CUT, binary quadratic optimization, and Ising models. The moment--sum-of-squares (Moment–SOS) hierarchy provides certified semidefinite relaxations that are often empirically exact at low order. We ask: once a relaxation is exact, how difficult is the resulting semidefinite program (SDP) to solve with first-order methods?

Exactness does not imply regularity. At every order \(d\ge 2\), a unique rank-one moment optimum is primal degenerate; moreover, if one optimal SOS certificate is strictly complementary, then the certificate set is positive-dimensional and contains singular boundary points. Thus first-order methods may converge to such singular points, around which pointwise analyses that assume regularity at the limit cannot establish a local linear convergence rate.

We show that, for exact Boolean Moment–SOS relaxations in their canonical quotient form, this degeneracy is nevertheless benign. We develop an abstract mechanism, which we call _residual-field rigidity_, that propagates regularity from the relative interior of the optimal set to its singular boundary. It requires neither the primal nor the dual optimal solution to be unique, and it is equivalent to the first-order stall directions of the residual coinciding with the tangent directions of the optimal set. For Boolean Moment–SOS, unique rank-one exactness and the existence of one strictly complementary certificate suffice to trigger this mechanism, yielding a uniform error bound around the entire optimal set. Consequently, ADMM, sGS–ADMM, and PDHG converge eventually linearly from every initialization, even when their limiting certificate is singular. Finally, outside a lower-dimensional semialgebraic exceptional set of Boolean objectives, these hypotheses hold simultaneously at every uniquely rank-one exact order.

## 1 Introduction ### Problem statement. Consider the pseudo-Boolean optimization (PBO): given a real polynomial _f_ in _n_ variables, compute \(\mathrm{OPT}(f):=\mathrm{min}_{x\in\{\pm 1\}^n}f(x).\) (1.1) Since \(x_i^2=1\) on the cube, we always represent _f_ by its unique square-free (multilinear) polynomial. Problem (1.1) is a broad modeling language for discrete optimization \[BH02\]. Already at degree two it contains MAX-CUT, unconstrained binary quadratic optimization (QUBO) \[KHG+14\], and ground states of Ising spin glasses, which are NP-hard to compute \[Bar82\]; higher degrees cover Boolean constraint satisfaction. Semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations have been central to this problem class since the Goemans-Williamson approximation algorithm for MAX-CUT \[GW95\]. ### The Moment-SOS hierarchy. The canonical family of semidefinite relaxations for (1.1) is the Moment-SOS hierarchy \[Las01, Par03, Lau03a\]. At order _d_, a true probability distribution on the cube is replaced by a degree-2_d_ pseudo-moment sequence, represented by a positive-semidefinite (PSD) moment matrix; the dual PSD variable is a sum-of-squares (SOS) Gram certificate. In the language of theoretical computer science, this is the degree-2_d_ pseudoexpectation / SOS proof-system view \[BS14, Moi20\]. The order-_d_ value _pd(f_) is defined at every _admissible_ order, \(2d\ge\mathrm{deg}f\), and satisfies \(p_d(f)\le\mathrm{OPT}(f),p_{d_\mathrm{min}}(f)\le p_{d_\mathrm{min}+1}(f)\le\cdots,d_\mathrm{min}(f):=\mathrm{max}\{1,\lceil\mathrm{deg}f/2\rceil\},\) (1.2) and the hierarchy is exact at order _n_ on the finite cube \[Lau03a\] (see also Theorem 6.1). We call the relaxation _exact_ at order _d_ if _pd(f_)=OPT(_f_), and _uniquely rank-one exact_ if in addition its moment SDP has the unique optimizer \(b_d(x_\star)b_d(x_\star)^\top\), where _x⋆_ is the Boolean minimizer and _bd_ is the monomial vector, as elaborated in §2. ### Worst-case looseness versus empirical low-order exactness. How large must _d_ be? Worst- case theory is discouraging: the cut polytope of the complete graph needs relaxation order \(\lceil n/2\rceil\) \[Lau03b\], knapsack-type instances carry \(\Omega(n)\) SOS-degree lower bounds \[Gri01\], and random _k_-CSPs keep large gaps even at order \(\Omega(n)\) \[Sch08\]. Computational practice tells a different story. On unconstrained binary quadratic optimization, order two often delivers the exact solution or a very good approximation \[HKS25\]. BQP relaxations are a standard testbed for scalable low-rank solvers \[YLCT23, HTT26, HTT25, WHX25\]. The second-order Boolean relaxation, reported empirically exact on random QUBO, has been solved at _n_=120 variables, a moment matrix of size 7,261 with about 17.9 million equality constraints \[WH25\], and certifiably exact low-order relaxations are routine in robotics and perception \[RCBL19, BKGJ18, YC22, KXS+24\]. Most hierarchy theory asks how large _d_ must be before exactness. The empirical picture motivates a complementary question: _Once a low-order Moment-SOS relaxation is exact,_
_how hard is the resulting semidefinite program to solve?_ ### Why first-order methods. For SDPs of small and medium size, interior-point methods are the solver of choice. They need few iterations \[DK02\] and reach high accuracy. Under strict complementarity they even converge locally superlinearly \[AHO98, LSZ98\]. But each conventional interior-point iteration forms and factors a dense matrix whose dimension is the number of equality constraints. First-order splitting methods target the large-scale regime where this matrix can no

<tbc>longer even be formed \[WGY10, OCPB16\]. Boolean moment relaxations sit squarely in that regime, with a moderate PSD block (the moment matrix of size 7,261 above) and equality constraints quadratic in its size (the 17.9 million above). A splitting iteration needs only one eigendecomposition of the moment matrix, plus an affine projection through a factorization computed once; its local convergence rate is therefore the relevant measure of hardness.

## Exact but degenerate.

Can a splitting method--ADMM \[GM76\], its symmetric Gauss-Seidel variant sGS-ADMM \[CST17\], or PDHG \[CP11\]--converge locally linearly on the exact relaxation? These methods are sublinear in the worst case \[DY17, ZAdK24\], and locally linear under regularity conditions at the limit point they select \[HSZ18, KJY25, Jia26, DLY26, LHL<sup>+</sup>26\]. Unfortunately, exact Boolean relaxations sit in a known harder class: _degenerate_ SDPs. Suppose _f_ has a unique Boolean minimizer _x<sub>⋆</sub>_ and order _d_ is uniquely rank-one exact, so the moment optimum is the single rank-one matrix \(X_\star=b_d(x_\star)b_d(x_\star)^\top\). Then, this optimum is primal degenerate whenever \(d\ge 2\), in the standard SDP sense \[AHO97\] (§2). Moreover, once one SOS certificate is strictly complementary--the generic case (§6)--the optimal Gram matrices form a positive-dimensional compact convex set S_<sub>⋆</sub>_ whose relative boundary consists of certificates that lose rank. A first-order method is free to converge to such a singular boundary certificate, where the pointwise regularity toolbox breaks down and no local linear rate can be concluded.

## Two unusual observations.

Practice, however, does not match this pessimism, and Figure 1 shows the phenomenon that motivates this paper. On the second-order moment relaxation of a BQP instance with _n_=20, exact ADMM started cold converges to a KKT point whose certificate is _not_ strictly complementary, yet the fixed-point residual still enters a sharp linear phase (Figure 1(a)). This behavior was recorded as an open question in \[KJY25\]. Nor is it an accident of one trajectory. On a second quotient instance, one hundred runs initialized near sampled _singular_ optimal fixed points (Figure 1(b)) all converge locally linearly (Figure 1(c)). A dual Riemannian method reports similar behavior on BQP relaxations \[WHX25\], and the effect persists for higher-degree objectives (Appendix H). For general degenerate SDPs, by contrast, the pessimism is justified by explicit examples that lose local linear convergence altogether \[Jia26, CST16, KY26b, KY26a\]. Exact Boolean relaxations thus appear to carry a hidden benign structure, which this paper identifies and proves.

## Main message: the degeneracy is benign.

Our headline result explains these observations: for exact Boolean Moment-SOS relaxations in the quotient form of Figure 1(b)-(c), constructed in §2, one strictly complementary certificate--anywhere in S_<sub>⋆</sub>_--is enough for the fast regime. The reason is a uniform _setwise_ error bound for the canonical Douglas-Rachford (DR) residual around the entire fixed-point set. It is produced by a mechanism we call _residual-field rigidity_: a positive first-order modulus of the residual field over the relative interior of the optimal set cannot vanish at its singular boundary. Equivalently, the directions along which the residual stalls to first order are exactly the directions along the optimal set, so the second-order slow regions of \[KY26b\] cannot form near it. Existing local linear-rate theory for splitting methods on SDPs and related conic programs is local to a regular KKT point. It assumes strict complementarity, nondegeneracy, or an error bound at the limit point the algorithm selects \[HSZ18, KJY25, Jia26, DLY26, LHL<sup>+</sup>26\]. Augmented Lagrangian methods are different, since one strictly complementary pair already yields the objective-level error bound they need \[LDZ24, CST16\]; the splitting residual does not inherit that bound (Theorem 4.4). Strict complementarity and nondegeneracy fail at the singular endpoints of a positive-dimensional certificate set. Rigidity replaces them by a condition that is checked at interior endpoints only; the regularity is _imported_ from there to the whole set. For the Boolean question above, unique rank-one exactness plus one strictly complementary certificate put the quotient relaxation in the fast regime of first-order methods; what remains open is the entrance time, which separates this rate statement from a complexity statement (§7). (Panel (a) uses the standard encoding; see §7.)

**Theorem 1.1** (Benign degeneracy, informal)**.** _Fix an order d at which the quotient Boolean moment SDP of §2 has a unique rank-one optimum and at least one strictly complementary optimal SOS certificate. Then, for every admissible step choice, the canonical DR residual satisfies a uniform local error bound around its entire fixed-point set. Consequently, ADMM, sGS-ADMM, and PDHG converge eventually linearly from every initialization, and the limiting KKT point they select need not be strictly complementary. Moreover, outside a lower-dimensional semialgebraic set in the_ 2_<sup>n</sup>-dimensional space of Boolean objectives, both hypotheses hold simultaneously at every uniquely rank-one exact order. The formal statements are Theorems 4.3 and 6.3 and Theorems 5.1 and 5.2._

## Contributions.

Our contributions are threefold.

(I) **Residual-field rigidity** (§3). For a semidefinite program with compact optimal sets and one strictly complementary optimal pair, where neither optimum need be unique, we prove that five properties of the Douglas-Rachford residual are equivalent. They are a uniform relative-interior derivative modulus, two finite kernel identities on the relative boundaries of the two optimal sets, a setwise error bound around the fixed-point set, a uniform modulus along every boundary normal, and exact first-order linearization at every endpoint. The proof uses exact projection secants instead of Taylor expansion at moving endpoints, and fixed anchors instead of spectral gaps. The theorem is Boolean-free. To our knowledge, it is the first error bound for a splitting residual on the semidefinite cone that holds uniformly around a positive-dimensional optimal set with singular boundary points; earlier bounds cover polyhedral, piecewise linear-quadratic, and well-posed conic feasibility problems \[PVZ21, ACL16\] or concern the objective rather than the splitting residual \[LDZ24, CST16\].<tbc>

(II) **Boolean verification** (§4). We verify the hypothesis of the rigidity theorem for exact Boolean Moment-SOS relaxations: two quotient-space identities--a constant-diagonal identity and an XOR-class identity--reduce the required relative-interior modulus to a finite-dimensional kernel computation and a compactness argument.<tbc>

(III) **Algorithmic transfer and genericity** (§5 and §6). We transfer the canonical error bound to ADMM, sGS-ADMM, and PDHG through residual rescalings and an affine endpoint chart; with averagedness in method-specific metrics, this yields the rates of Theorem 1.1. A separate semialgebraic argument establishes its generic half.

To our knowledge, the geometry of the exact regime at orders \(d\ge 2\) has not been used to analyze first-order solvers; Appendix A organizes the related work into four threads.

Appendix A discusses related work, Appendices B to G carry the deferred proofs, and Appendix H details the experiments.

All spaces are finite-dimensional and real. S_<sup>p</sup>_ is the space of symmetric \(p\times p\) matrices with the trace inner product \(\langle H_1,H_2\rangle=\text{tr}(H_1H_2)\), Frobenius norm \(\|\cdot\|_F\), and PSD cone \(\mathbb{S}_+^p\); \(\Pi_+\) is the Frobenius projection onto \(\mathbb{S}_+^p\) and \(\Pi_-:=\text{Id}-\Pi_+\). ## 2 Degeneracy of Exact Boolean Relaxations

This section makes the degeneracy phenomenon concrete; full proofs are in Appendix B.

### Boolean quotient moments.

Fix \(1\le d\le n\) and the Boolean ideal \(I_\mathrm{B}:=\langle x_1^2-1,\dots,x_n^2-1\rangle\), so that every polynomial has a unique square-free representative and \(x^Ax^B\equiv x^{A\triangle B}\), where \(\triangle\) is the symmetric difference. Index monomials by<tbc>

\(\mathcal{I}_d:=\{T\subseteq[n]:|T|\le\mathrm{min}\{d,n\}\},N_d:=|\mathcal{I}_d|,b_d(x):=(x^T)_{T\in\mathcal{I}_d}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_d};\) (2.1)

<tbc>when _d_ is fixed we write _N=N<sub>d</sub>_. For \(\Gamma\in\mathcal{I}_{2d}\), define the XOR-class matrices \((A_\Gamma)_{A,B}:=\mathbf{1}_{\{A\triangle B=\Gamma\}}\), indexed by \(A,B\in\mathcal{I}_d\). They have disjoint supports, are Frobenius orthogonal, and \(A_\emptyset=I_N\). A degree-2_d_ pseudo-moment sequence \(y=(y_\Gamma)_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{I}_{2d}}\) is encoded by the moment matrix<tbc>

\(M_d(y):=\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{I}_{2d}}y_\Gamma A_\Gamma,\text{i.e.}(M_d(y))_{A,B}=y_{A\triangle B},\) (2.2)

<tbc>and the feasible _moment body_ is the spectrahedron \(\mathcal{X}_d:=\{M_d(y):y_\emptyset=1,M_d(y)\unknown 0\}\). Writ ing \(C_f:=\sum_\Gamma f_\Gamma A_\Gamma/\|A_\Gamma\|_F^2\) for the canonical matrix representative of \(f=\sum_\Gamma f_\Gamma x^\Gamma\) (so that \(\langle C_f,M_d(y)\rangle=\sum_\Gamma f_\Gamma y_\Gamma\)), at every admissible order (\(\mathrm{deg}f\le 2d\)) the relaxation of (1.1) is<tbc>

\((\mathrm{P}_d)p_d(f):=\mathrm{min}_{X\in\mathcal{X}_d}\langle C_f,X\rangle.\) (2.3)

<tbc>The identity matrix is strictly feasible and X_<sub>d</sub>_ is compact, so the minimum is attained. Moreover, (P_<sub>d</sub>_) is a standard-form SDP under an explicit independent equality encoding A_<sub>d</sub>X=e_<sub>1</sub> of full row rank _m=N(N_+1)/2-|I<sub>2_d_</sub>|+1 (Theorem B.1). Its exact dual is the SOS problem: maximize \(\gamma\) subject to \(f-\gamma\equiv b_d(x)^\top Sb_d(x)\) (mod_I_<sub>B</sub>) with the Gram matrix \(S\unknown 0\) (Appendix B). When the relaxation is exact with value _f<sub>⋆</sub>_=OPT(_f_), the optimal Gram certificates form the set

\(\mathcal{S}_\star:=\{S\unknown 0:b_d(x)^\top Sb_d(x)\equiv f-f_\star(\mathrm{mod}I_\mathrm{B})\},\) (2.4)

which is compact because every \(S\in\mathcal{S}_\star\) has the same trace \(f_\emptyset-f_\star\) (Theorem B.2).

### Unique rank-one exactness.

If _f_ has a unique Boolean minimizer _x<sub>⋆</sub>_, define the first order of _unique rank-one exactness_,

\(d_\star(f):=\mathrm{min}\big\{1\le d\le n:\mathrm{deg}f\le 2d,\mathrm{argmin}(\mathrm{P}_d)=\{b_d(x_\star)b_d(x_\star)^\top\}\big\}.\) (2.5)

This is well defined with \(d_\star(f)\le n\), and it persists upward: unique rank-one exactness at _d_<sub>0</sub> implies it at every \(d_0\le d\le n\) (Theorem 6.1). Throughout the Boolean sections, §2 and §4-§5, we fix an order \(d\ge d_\star(f)\) and abbreviate \(X_\star=uu^\top=Nqq^\top\) with \(u:=b_d(x_\star)\in\{\pm 1\}^N\) and \(q:=u/\sqrt{N}\).

_Remark_ 2.1 (Symmetric objectives need a gauge). A unique Boolean minimizer excludes symmetric models such as MAX-CUT or zero-field Ising objectives, whose minimizers come in \(\pm\) pairs; they enter after a standard gauge fixing (fixing one spin), and we use them as motivation only.

### Merged squares and degeneracy.

Every optimal certificate annihilates _u_, since \(u^\top Su=f(x_\star)-f_\star=0\) and \(S\unknown 0\); so S_<sub>⋆</sub>_ lives on the cone \(\mathbb{S}_+(V):=\{S\unknown 0:\mathrm{ran}(S)\subseteq V\}\), where _U_:=ran(_X<sub>⋆</sub>_)=span{_q_} and \(V:=\mathrm{ker}(X_\star)=q^\perp\). Now let \(d\ge 2\), choose two coordinates \(i\neq j\), put _a_:=_x<sub>⋆,i</sub>x<sub>⋆,j</sub>_, and define two vectors in R_<sup>N</sup>_: \(w_1:=e_\emptyset-ae_{\{i,j\}}\) and _w_<sub>2</sub>:=_e_<sub>{_i_}</sub>-_ae_<sub>{_j_}</sub>. Both are orthogonal to _u_, and because \((x^{\{i,j\}})^2\equiv(x^{\{i\}})^2\equiv 1\), both rank-one Gram matrices represent the _same_ Boolean polynomial:

\(b_d(x)^\top w_1w_1^\top b_d(x)\equiv 2\big(1-ax_ix_j\big)\equiv b_d(x)^\top w_2w_2^\top b_d(x)(\mathrm{mod}I_\mathrm{B}).\) (2.6)

Quotienting by \(x_i^2=1\) thus merges distinct squares and creates nonzero _same-polynomial directions_ such as \(w_1w_1^\top-w_2w_2^\top\). These directions live in the subspace \(\mathcal{L}:=\mathrm{ran}(\mathcal{A}_d^*)\cap\mathbb{S}(V)\), where S(_V_) denotes the symmetric matrices supported on _V_ . Differences of optimal certificates always lie in L, and under strict complementarity L is the direction space of S_<sub>⋆</sub>_ (Theorem C.2).

**Proposition 2.2** (Primal degeneracy at every order \(d\ge 2\))**.** _For the independent encoding_ A_<sub>d</sub>, primal nondegeneracy of X<sub>⋆</sub> \[AHO97\] holds if and only if m=N, and_ \(\mathrm{dim}\mathcal{L}=m-N=\frac{N(N-1)}{2}-|\mathcal{I}_{2d}|+1\)_. At d_=1 _one has m=N; at every_ \(2\le d\le n\) _one has m\>N (indeed_ \(w_1w_1^\top-w_2w_2^\top\in\mathcal{L}\backslash\{0\}\)_), so the rank-one primal optimum is degenerate. If, in addition,_ S_<sub>⋆</sub> contains a_ strictly complementary _certificate S_<sub>sc</sub>_, i.e._ rank(_S_<sub>sc</sub>)=_N_-1_, then_ affS_<sub>⋆</sub>=S_<sub>sc</sub>+L_, so_ S_<sub>⋆</sub> is positive-dimensional with_ dimS_<sub>⋆</sub>=m-N._

The proof is in Appendix B. Degeneracy here concerns the optimum relative to the constraints rather than singularity of the matrix _X<sub>⋆</sub>_ itself. The encoding is always _injective_ on the tangent space of the rank-one PSD manifold, while nondegeneracy asks for _surjectivity_ onto R_<sup>m</sup>_.

### The geometric problem.

Suppose from now on that S_<sub>⋆</sub>_ contains one strictly complementary certificate _S_<sub>sc</sub>; equivalently, \(X_\star+S_\mathrm{sc}\succ 0\). Then \(\mathcal{S}_\star=(S_\mathrm{sc}+\mathcal{L})\cap\mathbb{S}_+(V)\) (Theorem C.2), a compact convex slice of the PSD cone supported on _V_ . The certificate _S_<sub>sc</sub> lies in the relative interior of this slice, every certificate on its relative boundary loses rank, and by Theorem 2.2 the boundary is nonempty for \(d\ge 2\). A first-order method is free to converge to any point of the slice; at a relative-boundary point, analyses that require strict complementarity at the selected limit do not apply, and general conic programming _does_ produce arbitrarily slow regions there \[KY26a\].

## 3 Residual-Field Rigidity

This section is Boolean-free. Theorem 3.1 below asks only for compact optimal sets and one strictly complementary pair; neither optimum needs to be unique. The result is a theorem that makes five<tbc>

properties of the residual field equivalent, among them a setwise error bound. §4 verifies one of them and inherits the other four. ## 3.1 The canonical residual and the two-sided geometry Consider the primal-dual pair \((\mathsf{P})\mathrm{min}_{X\unknown 0}\langle C,X\rangle\mathrm{s}.\mathrm{t}.\mathcal{A}X=b,\)

Set _U_:=ran_X_sc and _V_:=ran_S_sc=_U_\`, let _PU_, _PV_ be the orthogonal projectors onto them, write S(_U_), S(_V_) for the symmetric matrices supported on _U_, _V_ , and define the primal and dual direction spaces and their sum \(\mathcal{M}:=\mathcal{N}\cap\mathbb{S}(U),\mathcal{L}:=\mathcal{R}\cap\mathbb{S}(V),\mathcal{D}:=\mathcal{M}\oplus\mathcal{L}.\) (3.3) Every optimal _X_ is supported on _U_ and every optimal _S_ on _V_ , so (Theorem C.2, Appendix C.1) \(\mathcal{X}_\star=(X_\mathrm{sc}+\mathcal{M})\cap\mathbb{S}_+(U),\mathcal{S}_\star=(S_\mathrm{sc}+\mathcal{L})\cap\mathbb{S}_+(V),\mathcal{Z}_\star=\mathrm{Fix}T_{\sigma,1}=\mathcal{X}_\star-\sigma\mathcal{S}_\star.\) (3.4) We call the points of Z_⋆ endpoints_, where convergent runs end. Also aff \(\mathcal{Z}_\star=X_\mathrm{sc}-\sigma S_\mathrm{sc}+\mathcal{D}\), and \(\bar{Z}\in\mathrm{ri}\mathcal{Z}_\star\) exactly when \(\bar{X}\) is positive definite on _U_ and \(\bar{S}\) on _V_ . In words, Z_⋆_ is a product of two PSD slices, and its relative boundary consists of the endpoints at which a factor loses rank. When X_⋆_={_X⋆_} is a singleton, M={0} and D=L, which is the Boolean situation of §2. ## 3.2 Endpoints, derivatives, and the stall cone Fix an endpoint \(\bar{Z}=\bar{X}-\sigma\bar{S}\) and set \(K_\bar{X}:=\mathrm{ker}\bar{X}\cap U\) and \(K_\bar{S}:=\mathrm{ker}\bar{S}\cap V\) , the subspaces on which the two factors have lost rank; both are {0} exactly on riZ_⋆_. Only these kernels move with the endpoint; _U_ and _V_ stay fixed, and no continuity of eigenbases in the endpoint is ever assumed. At an interior endpoint the PSD projection is differentiable, and in the fixed \(U\oplus V\) blocks its derivative \(J_{\bar{X},\bar{S}}(H):=\Pi'_+(\bar{Z};H)\) keeps the _UU_ block, kills the _VV_ block, and replaces the cross block by the solution _Y_ of the Sylvester equation \(\bar{X}Y+\sigma Y\bar{S}Y=\bar{X}H_{UV}\) (3.5)

(Appendix C.2). Writing _J_ for \(J_{\bar{X},\bar{S}}\), the residual derivative is \(\delta'_\sigma(\bar{Z};H)=-\mathsf{P}J(H)-\mathsf{P}^\perp(H-J(H))\), with orthogonal components. Two cones organize everything that follows:

\(\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z}):=\{H\in\mathbb{S}^p:\delta'_\sigma(\bar{Z};H)=0\},T_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z}):=\text{the tangent cone of}\mathcal{Z}_\star\text{at}\bar{Z}.\) (3.6)

The first is the _stall cone_: the directions along which the residual vanishes to first order, so the first-order dynamics of the splitting method stalls \[KY26b\]; the second collects the directions along the optimal set. Always \(T_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})\subseteq\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})\), since \(\delta_\sigma\) vanishes on Z_<sub>⋆</sub>_; the question is whether the stall cone is _larger_ (Appendix D.7 relates this to the second-order limit dynamics of \[KY26b\]).

## 3.3 The rigidity theorem

Define the relative-interior and full-normal derivative moduli

\(\mu_\mathrm{ri}:=\mathrm{inf}_{\bar{Z}\in\mathrm{ri}\mathcal{Z}_\star H\in\mathcal{D}^\perp,\|H\|_F=1}\|\delta'_\sigma(\bar{Z};H)\|_F,\mu_\mathrm{nor}:=\mathrm{inf}_{\bar{Z}\in\mathcal{Z}_\star H\in N_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z}),\|H\|_F=1}\|\delta'_\sigma(\bar{Z};H)\|_F.\) (3.7)

**Theorem 3.2** (Two-sided rigidity and exact linearization)**.** _Under Theorem 3.1, the following are equivalent:_

(i) Uniform interior modulus: \(\mu_\mathrm{ri}>0\).<tbc>

(ii) Complementarity rigidity: _the_ primal identity _(left) holds for every_ \(\bar{S}\in\mathrm{rb}\mathcal{S}_\star\) _and the_ dual identity _(right) for every_ \(\bar{X}\in\mathrm{rb}\mathcal{X}_\star\)_, both named after the direction space they test:_<tbc>

\(\{E\in\mathcal{N}:P_VEP_V=0,E\bar{S}=0\}=\mathcal{M},\{F\in\mathcal{R}:P_UFP_U=0,\bar{X}F=0\}=\mathcal{L}.\) \(\text{(3.8)}\)

(iii) Setwise error bound: _there are_ \(c_\sigma,t_\sigma>0\) _with_<tbc>

\(\|\delta_\sigma(Z)\|_F\ge c_\sigma\mathrm{dist}_F(Z,\mathcal{Z}_\star)\text{\textit{whenever}}\mathrm{dist}_F(Z,\mathcal{Z}_\star)\le t_\sigma.\) \(\text{(3.9)}\)

(iv) Uniform normal modulus: \(\mu_\mathrm{nor}>0\).<tbc>

(v) Exact linearization: \(\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})=T_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})\) _for every_ \(\bar{Z}\in\mathrm{rb}\mathcal{Z}_\star\).

_Conditions (ii) and (v) hold automatically at relative-interior factors and endpoints, so requiring them everywhere is equivalent. Whether the conditions hold does not depend on_ \(\sigma\)_; the constants do. No positive lower bound on the nonzero eigenvalues of the varying optimal pair_ \((\bar{X},\bar{S})\) _is imposed._

### What each condition says.

_(i) Stiffness across the flat interior._ Transverse to the optimal set, the residual responds at first order, with a lower bound \(\mu_\mathrm{ri}\) that is uniform over the interior endpoints, however close they sit to the singular boundary. This is the verifiable condition. Interior endpoints are nonsingular matrices, where the residual is real-analytic with the explicit linear derivative (3.5), so checking (i) is linear algebra plus compactness; §4 does this. _(ii) Complementarity rigidity._ At an endpoint where one factor has lost rank, a direction can couple its vanished eigenspace with the support of the other factor, and the linearized residual does not see it. The two identities say that every such direction already runs along the optimal set. _(iii) The residual measures the distance._ In a tube around the optimal set, the KKT residual is at least a constant times the distance to it, which averaged splitting methods convert into linear rates (§5). _(iv) Stiffness along every normal._ At a singular endpoint the normal cone is larger than \(\mathcal{D}^\perp\), since directions leaving the PSD cone through a vanished eigenspace are normal there too; (iv) asks for the response of (i) along all these normals, with a bound uniform over all endpoints. _(v) Stall cone equals tangent cone._ The directions along which the residual vanishes to first order are exactly those along the optimal set; equivalently, no direction leaves Z_<sub>⋆</sub>_ while the first-order dynamics stalls--the geometric content of "benign".

### 3.4 Proof outline of Theorem 3.2

### Two obstacles.

A pointwise argument would differentiate the residual at the nearest endpoint; two features of the degenerate geometry defeat this. First, the _base moves_. Along a sequence \(Z_k\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}_\star\) the nearest endpoint \(\bar{Z}_k\) changes with _k_, and the projection derivative is discontinuous in the endpoint exactly where a kernel grows. So a Taylor expansion at \(\bar{Z}_k\) has no uniform remainder. Second, _eigenvalues vanish_. The positive eigenvalues of the moving optima \(\bar{X}_k\), \(\bar{S}_k\) can tend to zero, so any bound whose constant contains their reciprocals degenerates along the sequence.

### Proof outline.

We prove (i)\(\Rightarrow\)(ii)\(\Rightarrow\)(iii)\(\Rightarrow\)(iv)\(\Rightarrow\)(i) and (iii)\(\Rightarrow\)(v)\(\Rightarrow\)(ii). The step (ii)\(\Rightarrow\)(iii) carries the weight, and three devices handle the two obstacles.

_Fixed anchors_. Every uniform spectral estimate comes from the anchor pair, through \(a_X:=\lambda_{min}(X_{sc}|_U)\) and \(a_S:=\lambda_{min}(S_{sc}|_V)\). The Sylvester operator \(Y\mapsto X_{sc}|_UY+\sigma Y\bar{S}_{VV}\) has inverse norm at most \(a_X^{-1}\) for every optimal \(\bar{S}\), singular or not, and symmetrically with \((\sigma a_S)^{-1}\) (Theorem C.3). Together with the optimal-set radii of (D.1), these gaps bound every decomposition of a normal vector into a \(\mathcal{D}^\perp\) part and two kernel parts (Theorem D.2). The anchors also prove (i)\(\Rightarrow\)(ii): to test the primal identity at a boundary certificate \(\bar{S}\), form the interior endpoints \(X_{sc}-\sigma\bar{S}_\varepsilon\) with \(\bar{S}_\varepsilon=(1-\varepsilon)\bar{S}+\varepsilon S_{sc}\), whose primal factor is the anchor and whose dual factor is pushed toward its anchor. Along the push, the interior derivative of a direction _E_ from the left side of (3.8) converges to _E_ itself. Hence the residual derivative tends to zero, and (i) forces \(E\in\mathcal{D}\); the dual identity is symmetric (Appendix D.3).

_Exact secants_. For (ii)\(\Rightarrow\)(iii) we take _Z<sub>k</sub>_ with \(t_k:=dist_F(Z_k,\mathcal{Z}_\star)\rightarrow 0\) and residual _o(t<sub>k</sub>_), and we never differentiate. With \(\bar{Z}_k\) the nearest endpoint, the exact projections \(X_k=\Pi_+(Z_k)\) and \(S_k=-\sigma^{-1}\Pi_-(Z_k)\) define the secants \(E_k=(X_k-\bar{X}_k)/t_k\) and \(F_k=-\sigma(S_k-\bar{S}_k)/t_k\), which are bounded and sum to the unit normal \(H_k=(Z_k-\bar{Z}_k)/t_k\). These exact secants avoid a Taylor remainder at the moving endpoint. The small residual says \(\mathsf{P}E_k\rightarrow 0\) and \(\mathsf{P}^\perp F_k\rightarrow 0\), so \(\langle E_k,F_k\rangle\rightarrow 0\). Exact complementarity _X<sub>k</sub>S<sub>k</sub>_=0 gives the energy identity \(\langle E_k,F_k\rangle=\sigma t_k^{-2}(\langle X_k,\bar{S}_k\rangle+\langle\bar{X}_k,S_k\rangle)\ge 0\). Hence both complementarity gaps are \(o(t_k^2)\).

_The PSD product inequality_. For PSD _A,B_, \(\|AB\|_F^2\le\|A\|_{op}\|B\|_{op}\langle A,B\rangle\) (Theorem C.6). Applied to the two gaps, it gives \(\|X_k\bar{S}_k\|_F=o(t_k)\) and \(\|\bar{X}_kS_k\|_F=o(t_k)\), that is, \(E_k\bar{S}_k\rightarrow 0\) and \(\bar{X}_kF_k\rightarrow 0\). No eigenvalue bound enters here. The anchors remove the blocks on the wrong support, \((E_k)_{VV}\unknown 0\) and \((F_k)_{UU}\unknown 0\), since these pair to _o_(1) with _S_<sub>sc</sub> and _X_<sub>sc</sub>. The limits _E,F_ are therefore exactly the directions tested in (3.8), so \(E\in\mathcal{M}\), \(F\in\mathcal{L}\), and the limit _H=E+F_ of the unit normals lies in D. The anchor-controlled normal decomposition and the signs of the secants against the kernel cones then give a contradiction (Appendix D.4). The remaining implications are short (Appendix D.5). Differentiating the error bound along a normal gives (iii)\(\Rightarrow\)(iv), and the inclusion \(\mathcal{D}^\perp\subseteq N_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}\) at interior endpoints gives (iv)\(\Rightarrow\)(i). For (iii)\(\Rightarrow\)(v), a residual of order _o(t_) along \(\bar{Z}+tH\) forces \(dist_F(\bar{Z}+tH,\mathcal{Z}_\star)=o(t)\) through (3.9), so _H_ is tangent. For (v)\(\Rightarrow\)(ii), the projection derivative is computed at the two anchored endpoints, where it fixes primal test directions and annihilates dual ones. The PSD structure is essential (Theorems D.3 and D.4).

## 4 Boolean Verification of the Modulus

We now verify condition (i) of Theorem 3.2, the uniform interior modulus, for the Boolean moment SDP of §2; omitted computations are in Appendix E. Fix an order _d_ at which the relaxation is uniquely rank-one exact with a strictly complementary certificate, and instantiate §3 with _p=N_, \(X_{sc}=X_\star=Nqq^\top\), _U_=span{_q_}, \(V=q^\perp\), A=A_<sub>d</sub>_, _b=e_<sub>1</sub>, _C=C<sub>f</sub>_, and _X<sub>b</sub>=I<sub>N</sub>_. Here A_<sub>d</sub>_ is the independent encoding of Theorem B.1: its null space is the XOR-consistency direction space<tbc>

\(\mathcal{T}_d:=\mathrm{span}\{A_\Gamma:\emptyset\neq\Gamma\in\mathcal{I}_{2d}\}\) (every matrix in it has zero diagonal), and its row space is \(\mathcal{R}_d:=\mathcal{T}_d^\perp\). Compactness of S_<sub>⋆</sub>_ is the trace identity (Theorem B.2), and X_<sub>⋆</sub>_={_X<sub>⋆</sub>_} is a point, so Theorem 3.1 holds with M={0} and D=L, and the dual identity in (3.8) is automatic.

## 4.1 Two decisive subspace identities

**Lemma 4.1** (Boolean subspace geometry)**.** _With_ \(V=q^\perp\):

\(\mathbb{S}(V)^\perp=\{qv^\top+vq^\top:v\in\mathbb{R}^N\},\) (4.1)

\(\mathcal{T}_d\cap\mathbb{S}(V)^\perp=\{0\},\) (4.2)

\(\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{S}(V)\cap\mathcal{R}_d=\mathbb{S}(V)\cap\mathcal{H}_d^\perp,\mathcal{H}_d:=\mathrm{span}\{I_N\}\oplus\mathcal{T}_d.\) (4.3)

The first identity is elementary. The second is the _constant-diagonal identity_: a matrix \(qv^\top+vq^\top\in\mathcal{T}_d\) has zero diagonal 2_q<sub>A</sub>v<sub>A</sub>_ with every \(q_A=\pm N^{-1/2}\) nonzero, so _v_=0. The third is the _XOR-class identity_, built on \(uu^\top=\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathcal{I}_{2d}}x_\star^\Gamma A_\Gamma\); the full proofs are in Appendix E.1. In words: no consistency direction can lie in \(\mathbb{S}(V)^\perp\), and inside S(_V_) the equality row space and the Gram-map kernel agree.

## 4.2 A continuous extension of the interior derivative

For every \(S\in\mathcal{S}_\star\)--including boundary certificates--define the linear maps

\(\mathscr{J}_S(H):=h_{00}qq^\top+qw^\top+wq^\top,h_{00}:=q^\top Hq,w:=N(NI_N+\sigma S)^{-1}P_VHq,\Psi_S:=\mathsf{P}\mathscr{J}_S+\mathsf{P}^\perp(\mathrm{Id}-\mathscr{J}_S).\text{(4.4)}\)

The inverse exists because \(NI_N+\sigma S\unknown NI_N\), and \(S\mapsto\Psi_S\) is operator-norm continuous on all of S_<sub>⋆</sub>_. For \(S\in\mathrm{ri}\mathcal{S}_\star\) the projection is differentiable at \(X_\star-\sigma S\) and \(\Pi'_+(X_\star-\sigma S;\cdot)=\mathscr{J}_S\), so \(\delta'_\sigma(X_\star-\sigma S;\cdot)=-\Psi_S\). At a boundary certificate the true directional derivative acquires exactly one extra nonlinear term, \(Q_K\Pi_+(Q_K^\top HQ_K)Q_K^\top\) with _Q<sub>K</sub>_ an orthonormal basis of \(K:=\mathrm{ker}(S)\cap V\) (Appendix E.2). So \(\Psi_S\) is a continuous _algebraic extension_ of the interior derivative.

**Proposition 4.2** (Uniform relative-interior modulus)**.** _For every_ \(S\in\mathcal{S}_\star\), \(\mathrm{ker}(\Psi_S)=\mathcal{L}\)_; consequently_

\(\mu_\mathrm{ri}\ge\mu_\star:=\mathrm{min}_{S\in\mathcal{S}_\star}\sigma_\mathrm{min}\big(\Psi_S\big|_{\mathcal{L}^\perp}\big)>0.\) (4.5)

The proof (Appendix E.3) is a kernel chain through the two identities. If \(\Psi_S(H)=0\), the two residual components vanish separately. The constant-diagonal identity (4.2) then forces \(\mathscr{J}_S(H)\in\mathcal{T}_d\cap\mathbb{S}(V)^\perp=\{0\}\), and unwinding (4.4) places _H_ in \(\mathbb{S}(V)\cap\mathcal{R}_d=\mathcal{L}\). Continuity of \(S\mapsto\Psi_S\) and compactness of S_<sub>⋆</sub>_ turn the pointwise kernel statement into the uniform bound (4.5).

## 4.3 The deterministic theorem

**Theorem 4.3** (Deterministic Boolean benign degeneracy)**.** _Suppose the order-d Boolean moment relaxation has a unique rank-one optimum and one strictly complementary optimal SOS certificate. Then, for every fixed_ \(\sigma>0\)_, the canonical DR residual satisfies the setwise error bound_ (3.9) _around its entire fixed-point set_ Z_<sub>⋆</sub>, and its stall cone equals the tangent cone of_ Z_<sub>⋆</sub> at every endpoint. The algorithmic conclusions of Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 hold for the independent encoding_ (B.3)_, at every endpoint, regardless of the rank of the certificate selected by the iteration._

_Proof._ Theorem B.1 gives surjectivity of A_<sub>d</sub>_ and Theorem B.2 compactness of S_<sub>⋆</sub>_; the instantiation above places us under Theorem 3.1; Theorem 4.2 verifies condition (i) of Theorem 3.2, whose condition (iii) is the error bound and condition (v) the exact linearization. Then apply §5.

_Remark_ 4.4 (Uniqueness cannot be dropped in the Boolean theorem). Theorem 3.2 needs no uniqueness, but Theorem 4.3 does. For _f(x_)=1-_x_<sub>1</sub> on \(\{\pm 1\}^2\) at full order, the two minimizers \((1,\pm 1)\) make both X_<sub>⋆</sub>_ and S_<sub>⋆</sub>_ segments, and a strictly complementary pair exists. Take the endpoint whose primal factor is the moment matrix of the point mass at the first minimizer. Along the cross direction that couples the second minimizer with a nonminimizer, the residual is of order \(2t^2/\sigma\) while the distance to Z_<sub>⋆</sub>_ is \(\sqrt{2}t\) (Appendix E.5). The dual identity fails there, and the direction lies in \(\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})\backslash T_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})\). The same happens for every nonconstant full-order objective with two or more minimizers. Unique rank-one exactness rules out such directions.

## 5 Consequences for Splitting Methods

This section converts the error bound (3.9) into convergence rates for exact ADMM, exact sGS- ADMM, and fixed-step PDHG; details are in Appendix F.

### ADMM and exact sGS-ADMM share one shadow map.

Exact ADMM on the dual SDP with penalty \(\sigma>0\) and multiplier step \(\tau>0\), and its exact symmetric Gauss-Seidel variant \[GM76, CST17\], both reduce to one common recursion in the shadow coordinate \(Z^k:=\mathsf{P}^\perp X^k+X_b-\sigma\mathsf{P}S^k-\sigma\mathsf{P}^\perp C\). The recursion is \(Z^{k+1}=T_{\sigma,\tau}(Z^k)\) with \(T_{\sigma,\tau}-\mathrm{Id}=-\mathsf{D}_\tau(r^\|+r_\sigma^\perp)\) and \(\mathsf{D}_\tau:=\mathsf{P}+\tau\mathsf{P}^\perp\) (established in \[KY26a\]; re-derived in Appendix F.2). The multiplier step only rescales the two orthogonal residual components, so, with \(\delta_{\sigma,\tau}:=T_{\sigma,\tau}-\mathrm{Id}\),

\(\|\delta_{\sigma,\tau}(Z)\|_F\ge\mathrm{min}\{1,\tau\}\|\delta_\sigma(Z)\|_F\ge\mathrm{min}\{1,\tau\}c_\sigma\mathrm{dist}_F(Z,\mathcal{Z}_\star)\) (5.1)

throughout the tube of (3.9): the setwise error bound transfers verbatim. For \(0<\tau<2\), \(T_{\sigma,\tau}\) is \(\mathrm{max}\{1,\tau\}/2\)-averaged in the parameter-dependent metric \(\mathsf{G}_\tau:=\mathsf{P}+\tau^{-1}\mathsf{P}^\perp\), which is equivalent to the Frobenius metric (Theorem F.2, Appendix F.3; cf. \[KY26a\]).

### PDHG admits an endpoint chart.

Fixed-step PDHG \[CP11\] on (3.1), with state \(w=(X,\lambda)\) and steps \(\eta_x,\eta_y>0\), iterates \(X^+=\Pi_+(X-\eta_x(C-\mathcal{A}^*\lambda))\), \(\lambda^+=\lambda+\eta_y(b-\mathcal{A}(2X^+-X))\). Consider the affine change of variables \(\Phi(X,\lambda)=(Z,r)\) with \(Z:=X-\eta_x(C-\mathcal{A}^*\lambda)\) and _r_:=A_X-b_. It is a bijection sending the fixed-point set W_<sub>⋆</sub>_:=Fix_T_<sub>P</sub> of the PDHG map _T_<sub>P</sub> onto \(\mathcal{Z}_\star\times\{0\}\), with Z_<sub>⋆</sub>_ the canonical fixed-point set at parameter \(\sigma=\eta_x\). In this chart the PDHG residual _factors through the canonical one_: there is an explicit linear isomorphism \(\mathsf{L}_{\eta_x,\eta_y}:\mathcal{R}\times\mathcal{N}\times\mathbb{R}^m\rightarrow\mathbb{S}^p\times\mathbb{R}^m\) with

\(\Phi T_\mathsf{P}\Phi^{-1}(Z,r)-(Z,r)=\mathsf{L}_{\eta_x,\eta_y}\big(r^\|(Z),r_{\eta_x^\perp}^\perp(Z),r\big)\) (5.2)

(Theorem F.3). Invertibility of \(\mathsf{L}_{\eta_x,\eta_y}\) and of the chart converts (3.9) into a native setwise error bound for PDHG, and _T_<sub>P</sub> is firmly nonexpansive in the standard preconditioned metric whenever \(\eta_x\eta_y\|\mathcal{A}\|_\mathrm{op}^2<1\) \[CP11, OV20\] (Theorem F.4).

### From error bound to rates.

The passage from a setwise error bound to convergence rates is standard averaged-operator theory \[BC17\]. For an \(\alpha\)-averaged map in a metric equivalent to the Euclidean one, a setwise error bound on a neighborhood of the fixed-point set makes every orbit converge to a fixed point. The distance then contracts eventually Q-linearly in that metric, and the iterates converge R-linearly (Theorem F.1, stated and proved quantitatively in Appendix F.1).

**Corollary 5.1** (ADMM and sGS-ADMM)**.** _Under the hypotheses of Theorem 4.3 (or, abstractly, Theorem 3.1 plus any condition of Theorem 3.2), for every fixed_ \(\sigma>0\) _and_ \(0<\tau<2\)_, the shadow_<tbc>

_orbits of exact ADMM and exact sGS-ADMM converge to an endpoint of_ Z_<sub>⋆</sub>. The distance contracts eventually Q-linearly in the_ \(\mathsf{G}_\tau\) _metric, and the shadow and the raw primal-dual iterates converge R-linearly (Appendix F.3)._

**Corollary 5.2** (PDHG)**.** _Under the same hypotheses with_ \(\sigma=\eta_x\) _and_ \(\eta_x\eta_y\|\mathcal{A}\|_\mathrm{op}^2<1\)_, every PDHG orbit converges to a KKT pair; the distance to_ W_<sub>⋆</sub> contracts eventually Q-linearly in the preconditioned metric, and the iterates and the slack_ \(S^k=C-\mathcal{A}^*\lambda^k\) _converge R-linearly._

The convergence is _eventual_: it begins after an entrance time that we do not bound (Appendix F.1).

## 6 Generic Benign Degeneracy

It remains to show that the two hypotheses of Theorem 4.3 occur broadly: outside one lower- dimensional semialgebraic set of objectives, they hold _simultaneously at every uniquely rank-one exact order_ (proofs in Appendix G).

### Full order: exactness and strict complementarity for free.

Let \(\mathcal{P}_n:=\mathrm{span}\{x^T:T\subseteq[n]\}\) be the 2_<sup>n</sup>_-dimensional space of square-free objectives, and \(\mathcal{P}_{\le 2d}\) its subspace of degree at most 2_d_.

**Proposition 6.1** (Full-order structure)**.** _At d=n the moment body_ X_<sub>n</sub> is the affine image, with unique coefficients, of the probability simplex on_ \(\{\pm 1\}^n\): \(X=\sum_{a\in\{\pm 1\}^n}\pi_ab_n(a)b_n(a)^\top\) _with_ \(\pi_a\ge 0\), \(\sum_a\pi_a=1\)_. Consequently every uniquely minimized f is uniquely rank-one exact at d=n, so_ \(d_\star(f)\le n\)_; and unique rank-one exactness persists upward from any order at which it holds. Moreover, for every uniquely minimized f the full-order relaxation admits a strictly complementary optimal certificate of rank_ 2_<sup>n</sup>_-1 _(Appendix G.1)._

### Fixed-order cells and one Gram construction.

Fix a candidate optimizer \(a\in\{\pm 1\}^n\) and an order _d_, and let _u=b<sub>d</sub>(a_). Inside the normalized coefficient space \(\mathcal{Q}(a,d):=\{g\in\mathcal{P}_{\le 2d}:g(a)=0\}\), the _exact cell_ E(_a,d_) collects the _g_ for which (P_<sub>d</sub>_) has the unique optimizer \(uu^\top\). The _strictly complementary cell_ \(\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d)\subseteq\mathcal{E}(a,d)\) collects the _g_ represented by some PSD Gram matrix _S_ with ker(_S_)=span{_u_}. For each nonempty \(\Gamma\in\mathcal{I}_{2d}\), split \(\Gamma=P_\Gamma\dot{\cup}Q_\Gamma\) into parts of size at most _d_ (with \(P_\Gamma=\Gamma\), \(Q_\Gamma=\emptyset\) when \(|\Gamma|\le d\)) and set

\(w_\Gamma:=e_{P_\Gamma}-a^\Gamma e_{Q_\Gamma},S_\mathrm{int}:=\sum_{\emptyset\neq A\in\mathcal{I}_d}w_Aw_A^\top.\) (6.1)

Each \(w_\Gamma\) is orthogonal to _u_ and its Gram matrix represents \(2(1-a^\Gamma x^\Gamma)\); under this splitting convention, the _N_-1 vectors \(w_A=e_A-a^Ae_\emptyset\) (\(\emptyset\neq A\in\mathcal{I}_d\)) form a basis of \(u^\perp\), so \(S_\mathrm{int}\unknown 0\) is an _interior certificate_ with kernel exactly span{_u_}.

**Theorem 6.2** (Fixed-order SC genericity)**.** E<sub>sc</sub>(_a,d_) _is open in_ Q(_a,d_) _and dense relative to_ E(_a,d); both cells are semialgebraic; and_ \(\mathrm{dim}\big(\mathcal{E}(a,d)\backslash\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d)\big)<\mathrm{dim}\mathcal{E}(a,d)\).

The proof (Appendix G.2) gets openness from the Gram construction (6.1), density from \(S+\varepsilon S_\mathrm{int}\), and the rest from Tarski-Seidenberg and the frontier theorem \[BCR98\].

### Ambient genericity.

To pass to P_<sub>n</sub>_, remove two bad families. The tie hyperplanes {_f:f(a_)=_f(b_)}, \(a\neq b\), contain every objective with a nonunique minimizer. For each (_a,d_), the objectives with \(f-f(a)\in\mathcal{E}(a,d)\backslash\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d)\) have closure dimension below 2_<sup>n</sup>_ by Theorem 6.2. This proves:

**Theorem 6.3** (Generic benign degeneracy)**.** _There exists an open dense semialgebraic set_ \(\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{gen}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_n\) _(so its complement has measure zero) such that every_ \(f\in\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{gen}\) _has a unique Boolean minimizer,_ \(d_\star(f)\le n\) _is well defined, and at every order_ \(d_\star(f)\le d\le n\) _the moment relaxation has the unique optimum_ \(b_d(x_\star)b_d(x_\star)^\top\) _and an optimal certificate of rank N<sub>d</sub>_-1_. Consequently, for every such f, every such order d, and every fixed admissible parameter choice, the conclusions of Theorems 4.3, 5.1 and 5.2 hold: the three splitting methods converge eventually linearly from every initialization._

_Proof._ Theorem G.1 constructs G<sub>gen</sub>; for \(f\in\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{gen}\) and \(d\in[d_\star(f),n]\) the hypotheses of Theorem 4.3 hold and §5 applies, for every \(\sigma>0\), since the argument of §4 gives a positive modulus for each \(\sigma\).

## 7 Conclusion

We proved that the degeneracy of exact Boolean Moment-SOS relaxations, in the quotient form of §2, is benign for first-order splitting methods, answering for that formulation the open question of \[KJY25\]. Under unique rank-one exactness and one strictly complementary certificate, the abstract rigidity theorem yields a setwise error bound around the optimal set. The three splitting methods therefore converge eventually linearly from every initialization, whichever certificate they select. Generically, the hypotheses hold at every uniquely rank-one exact order.

### Limitations.

Our guarantee concerns the algorithmic residual, not objective-function growth. It is a convergence-rate statement rather than a complexity theorem, with instance-dependent constants, no bound on the entrance time, and exact algorithms with fixed scalar parameters only. The rigidity abstract theorem removes primal uniqueness; yet the Boolean theorem cannot (Theorem 4.4). The verification is tied to the Boolean quotient through the two identities of Theorem 4.1. Redundant encodings (Figure 1(a)), sparse, symmetry-reduced, or constrained hierarchies change the quotient algebra, and the propagation can fail outside it (Theorem D.3; \[KY26a\]).

### Open problems.

First, a _quantitative_ rigidity: our constants come from compactness; we conjecture that for the Boolean class they admit explicit instance-parameter bounds, the missing step from rate separation to complexity separation. Second, _beyond the Boolean quotient_: which exact relaxations satisfy the two kernel identities of Theorem 3.2? We believe residual-field rigidity is the right abstraction for exact relaxations with degenerate optimal sets, and we hope it extends beyond the Boolean cube.

## A Related Work

§1 cites prior work in context; this appendix organizes it into four threads.

### Pseudo-Boolean optimization.

PBO is a classical umbrella for discrete optimization \[BH02, KHG<sup>+</sup>14\]. Two classical paradigms use semidefinite relaxations: exact solvers that combine branch- and-bound with polyhedral or SDP bounds \[RRW10\], and approximation algorithms built on SDP rounding \[GW95\]. When these approaches use an SDP relaxation, our result concerns the cost of _solving_ it rather than the cost of rounding or branching.

### Moment-SOS for PBO.

The hierarchy and its 0-1 specializations are classical \[Las01, Par03, Lau03a\]; books and surveys include \[Las09, BPT13, BS14, Moi20\]. Finite convergence and solution extraction are well studied: on the finite cube full order is always exact, generic problems enjoy finite convergence \[Nie14\], and flatness conditions certify exactness and permit extraction \[CF05\]. On the negative side, the worst-case lower bounds cited in §1 \[Lau03b, Gri01, Sch08\] show that no fixed order suffices for all instances, and sum-of-squares lower bounds extend to average-case problems such as planted clique \[BHK<sup>+</sup>19\]. The empirical low-order-exactness literature \[HKS25, WH25, KJY25, YLCT23\] motivates our conditional-on-exactness viewpoint. To our knowledge, the geometry of the _exact_ regime at orders \(d\ge 2\)--unique rank-one moment optimum, primal degeneracy, a generically positive-dimensional certificate set--has not been used to analyze first-order solvers.

### Error bounds and other solvers for degenerate SDP.

The regularity picture for splitting methods was summarized in §1. Other solvers rest on different conditions. Augmented Lagrangian methods converge linearly in their outer loop once a strictly complementary pair _exists_ and the subproblems are solved accurately enough \[Roc76a, Roc76b, LDZ24\]. The reason is quadratic growth of the primal and dual objectives, which for SDP follows from one such pair with compact solution sets \[LDZ24\]. Second-order growth is also the standing assumption of the multiple-solution ALM analysis of \[CST16\], and growth of a convex objective is equivalent to the proximal error bound and to linear rates of proximal methods \[DL18\]. The cost then moves into the subproblems. Generic first-order inner solvers are again worst-case sublinear, and the fast low-rank factorized route \[BM03\] needs a unique, strictly complementary primal optimum ("primal simplicity", see below) and a local initialization \[DLY25\]. Spectral bundle methods \[HR00\] are linear under strict complementarity and sufficient _rank capture_; the capture requirement is set by the kernel of the limiting dual slack, which can be large for degenerate SDPs even when the primal optimum has rank one \[DG23\]. For semidefinite feasibility sets without Slater-type regularity, the general guarantee is a Hölder bound with exponent tied to the singularity degree \[Stu00\]; see also \[ZS17\] for nuclear-norm problems. Splitting methods are governed by a different quantity, the Douglas-Rachford fixed-point residual. An error bound on this residual gives linear convergence of Douglas-Rachford and ADMM, and it is known for piecewise linear-quadratic and well-posed conic feasibility problems \[PVZ21, ACL16\]. For SDP, objective growth does not imply it: the tied-objective instance of Appendix E.5 meets the augmented Lagrangian hypotheses, yet its Douglas-Rachford residual bound fails. Complementarity rigidity is exactly what separates the two cases (Theorem 3.2).

### Setwise versus pointwise guarantees.

Our result differs from the pointwise analyses cited in §1 in two ways. First, the guarantee is _setwise_, so the endpoint the algorithm selects need satisfy neither strict complementarity nor nondegeneracy. Second, the regularity is _imported_, from a uniform interior modulus to every singular boundary endpoint. The bound (3.9) is a linear growth condition on the<tbc>

DR residual made uniform over the fixed-point set, and by Theorem 3.2 it is equivalent to the stall cone equaling the tangent cone at every endpoint. The companion paper \[KY26b\] studies the failure of this equality at a selected endpoint. There the gap \(\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})\backslash T_{\mathcal{Z}_*}(\bar{Z})\) consists of the two cross blocks coupling \(\mathrm{ran}\bar{X}\) with \(K_\bar{S}\) and \(K_\bar{X}\) with \(\mathrm{ran}\bar{S}\) (its Proposition 3), and each direction in it carries a nonzero second-order drift (its Proposition 6). Linear growth at \(\bar{Z}\) closes the gap (its Corollary 1(3)). The identities (3.8) say that these cross blocks are empty at every relative-boundary factor, and (iii)\(\Leftrightarrow\)(v) is the setwise converse of that corollary. The one-sided case, a unique primal optimum plus one strictly complementary pair, is the _primal simplicity_ condition of \[DU21, Definition 5\]; the two-sided theorem drops the uniqueness. In general conic programs, ADMM, sGS-ADMM, and PDHG can become arbitrarily slow near degenerate optima \[KY26a, Jia26\]; exact Boolean relaxations exclude this near their optimal set, with instance-dependent constants (§7).

## C.3 Two uniform Sylvester estimates

**Lemma C.3** (Sylvester estimates)**.** _Let_ \(A\in\mathbb{S}_+(U)\) _and_ \(B\in\mathbb{S}_+(V)\) _be given in the fixed bases, and let_ \(\mathsf{Syl}:Y\mapsto AY+\sigma YB\) _act on_ \(\mathrm{dim}U\times\mathrm{dim}V\) _matrices._

(a) _If_ \(A\unknown aI\) _with a\>_0_, then_ Syl _is invertible and_ \(\|\mathsf{Syl}^{-1}\|_{F\rightarrow F}\le a^{-1}\)_, uniformly over all_ \(B\unknown 0\).<tbc>

(b) _If_ \(B\unknown bI\) _with b\>_0_, then_ Syl _is invertible and_ \(\|\mathsf{Syl}^{-1}\|_{F\rightarrow F}\le(\sigma b)^{-1}\)_, uniformly over all_ \(A\unknown 0\).

_In particular, let_ \(a_X:=\lambda_\mathrm{min}(X_\mathrm{sc}|_U)\) _and_ \(a_S:=\lambda_\mathrm{min}(S_\mathrm{sc}|_V)\)_. The Sylvester operators of the primal- anchored endpoints have inverse norm at most_ \(a_X^{-1}\) _for every_ \(\bar{S}\in\mathcal{S}_\star\)_. Those of the dual-anchored endpoints have inverse norm at most_ \((\sigma a_S)^{-1}\) _for every_ \(\bar{X}\in\mathcal{X}_\star\).

_Proof._ For every _Y_ , \(\langle Y,\mathsf{Syl}Y\rangle=\mathrm{tr}(Y^\top AY)+\sigma\mathrm{tr}(Y^\top YB)\), and both terms are nonnegative. ## C.4 Two-sided tangent and normal cones

For an endpoint \(\bar{Z}=\bar{X}-\sigma\bar{S}\) define the two kernel-supported PSD cones \(\mathcal{K}(\bar{X}):=\{W\in\mathbb{S}_+^p:\mathrm{ran}W\subseteq K_\bar{X}\}\) and \(\mathcal{K}(\bar{S}):=\{W\in\mathbb{S}_+^p:\mathrm{ran}W\subseteq K_\bar{S}\}\).

**Proposition C.4** (Endpoint cones)**.** _Under Theorem 3.1, at_ \(\bar{Z}=\bar{X}-\sigma\bar{S}\in\mathcal{Z}_\star\),

\(T_{\mathcal{X}_\star}(\bar{X})=\{M\in\mathcal{M}:P_{K_\bar{X}}MP_{K_\bar{X}}\unknown 0\},N_{\mathcal{X}_\star}(\bar{X})=\mathcal{M}^\perp-\mathcal{K}(\bar{X}),\) (C.8)

\(T_{\mathcal{S}_\star}(\bar{S})=\{\Lambda\in\mathcal{L}:P_{K_\bar{S}}\Lambda P_{K_\bar{S}}\unknown 0\},N_{\mathcal{S}_\star}(\bar{S})=\mathcal{L}^\perp-\mathcal{K}(\bar{S}),\) (C.9)

\(T_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})=T_{\mathcal{X}_\star}(\bar{X})-\sigma T_{\mathcal{S}_\star}(\bar{S}),N_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})=\mathcal{D}^\perp-\mathcal{K}(\bar{X})+\mathcal{K}(\bar{S}),\) (C.10)

_where the sums are Minkowski sums and all cones are taken in_ S_<sup>p</sup>._

_Proof._ For the cone supported on _U_, the tangent and ambient normal formulas are

\(T_{\mathbb{S}_+(U)}(\bar{X})=\{H\in\mathbb{S}(U):P_{K_\bar{X}}HP_{K_\bar{X}}\unknown 0\},N_{\mathbb{S}_+(U)}(\bar{X})=\mathbb{S}(U)^\perp-\mathcal{K}(\bar{X}).\)

The tangent condition is necessary, as one sees by evaluating feasible secants on vectors of \(K_\bar{X}\). It is sufficient for the following reason. Adding \(\varepsilon P_{K_\bar{X}}\) to a direction _H_ makes its kernel block positive definite. The Schur complement then shows that \(\bar{X}+t(H+\varepsilon P_{K_\bar{X}})\) is PSD for small _t\>_0. Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow 0\) closes the cone. The normal formula is the polar: the free cross and range blocks force the corresponding normal blocks to vanish, and the polar of the PSD kernel cone is its negative. For the slice \(\mathcal{X}_\star=(X_\mathrm{sc}+\mathcal{M})\cap\mathbb{S}_+(U)\) the same approximation can be performed inside M. Replace _H_ by \(H+\varepsilon(X_\mathrm{sc}-\bar{X})\), whose kernel block is positive definite because \(X_\mathrm{sc}\succ 0\) on _U_. The relative Slater point _X_<sub>sc</sub> justifies the normal-cone intersection rule \[Roc15\]. Hence \(N_{\mathcal{X}_\star}(\bar{X})=\mathcal{M}^\perp+\mathbb{S}(U)^\perp-\mathcal{K}(\bar{X})=\mathcal{M}^\perp-\mathcal{K}(\bar{X})\), using \(\mathcal{M}\subseteq\mathbb{S}(U)\). This proves (C.8), and (C.9) is the same argument on _V_ with the anchor _S_<sub>sc</sub>.

For the product, the map \((X,S)\mapsto X-\sigma S\) is a linear isomorphism of \(\mathbb{S}(U)\times\mathbb{S}(V)\) onto \(\mathbb{S}(U)\oplus\mathbb{S}(V)\), so it carries the tangent cone of \(\mathcal{X}_\star\times\mathcal{S}_\star\), which is the product of the tangent cones, onto \(T_{\mathcal{X}_\star}(\bar{X})-\sigma T_{\mathcal{S}_\star}(\bar{S})\). For the normal cone, \(H\in N_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})\) if and only if \(\langle H,X-\bar{X}\rangle\le 0\) for all \(X\in\mathcal{X}_\star\) and \(\langle H,S-\bar{S}\rangle\ge 0\) for all \(S\in\mathcal{S}_\star\) (take \(S=\bar{S}\) for the first inequality and \(X=\bar{X}\) for the second), that is, \(H\in N_{\mathcal{X}_\star}(\bar{X})\cap\big(-N_{\mathcal{S}_\star}(\bar{S})\big)=(\mathcal{M}^\perp-\mathcal{K}(\bar{X}))\cap(\mathcal{L}^\perp+\mathcal{K}(\bar{S}))\). The proof gives positive constants \(\mu_\mathrm{nor},c_\sigma,t_\sigma\) for the fixed instance, but does not identify them with \(\mu_\mathrm{ri}\) or furnish a uniform rate over objectives. ### D.7 Relation to second-order limit dynamics

The stall cone \(\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})\) of (3.6) is the central object of the companion analysis \[KY26b\], which studies ADMM near an arbitrary KKT point under the same strict-complementarity assumption. There, \(\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})\) is the fixed-point set of the local first-order dynamics. Every direction \(H\in\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})\backslash T_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})\) drives a second-order limit drift \(\phi(\bar{Z};H)\neq 0\) (its Proposition 6). Along such a direction the residual decays like _t_<sup>2</sup> while the distance to the optimal set stays of order _t_; these are the slow regions seen in practice. That paper proves that a local linear growth condition at \(\bar{Z}\) forces \(\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})=T_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})\) (its Corollary 1(3)) and conjectures that the equality is necessary for local linear convergence. Theorem 3.2 supplies the converse in the setwise form: the equality at every endpoint of a compact fixed-point set is _equivalent_ to the uniform error bound (iii). In words, benign degeneracy means that no endpoint carries a direction of \(\mathcal{C}(\bar{Z})\backslash T_{\mathcal{Z}_\star}(\bar{Z})\), along which the residual is of second order while the distance is of first order. §4 shows that exact Boolean relaxations have none, and Theorem 4.4 exhibits one for nonconstant full-order Boolean objectives with tied minimizers.

### F.1 Error bound plus averagedness: the rate lemma

**Lemma F.1** (Setwise error bound plus averagedness)**.** _Let T be_ \(\alpha\)_-averaged,_ \(0<\alpha<1\)_, in a norm_ \(\|\cdot\|_G\) _with_ \(g_\mathrm{min}\|\cdot\|^2\le\|\cdot\|_G^2\le g_\mathrm{max}\|\cdot\|^2\), \(0<g_\mathrm{min}\le g_\mathrm{max}\)_, on a finite-dimensional space, suppose_ \(\mathrm{Fix}T\neq\emptyset\)_, and suppose_ \(\|Tz-z\|\ge c\mathrm{dist}(z,\mathrm{Fix}T)\) _whenever_ \(\mathrm{dist}(z,\mathrm{Fix}T)\le t_0\)_. Then every orbit converges to a point of_ Fix_T; it eventually enters the error-bound neighborhood, after which_ dist_<sub>G</sub>(z<sup>k</sup>,_Fix_T_) _contracts Q-linearly and the iterates converge R-linearly._

We prove the following quantitative form. Under the hypotheses of Theorem F.1, an orbit starting with \(\mathrm{dist}(z^0,\mathrm{Fix}T)\le t_0\sqrt{g_\mathrm{min}/g_\mathrm{max}}\) satisfies

\(\mathrm{dist}_G(z^k,\mathrm{Fix}T)\le\rho^k\mathrm{dist}_G(z^0,\mathrm{Fix}T),\rho^2=1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\bar{c}^2\frac{g_\mathrm{min}}{g_\mathrm{max}}\in(0,1),\) (F.1)

for any \(0<\bar{c}\le c\) small enough that \(\rho>0\). In the Euclidean norm, \(\mathrm{dist}(z^k,\mathrm{Fix}T)\le\sqrt{g_\mathrm{max}/g_\mathrm{min}}\rho^k\mathrm{dist}(z^0,\mathrm{Fix}T)\), and the iterates converge R-linearly to a point of Fix_T_. Every orbit converges to a fixed point and eventually enters such a neighborhood, so the conclusions hold eventually from any initialization.

_Proof._ The averagedness inequality \[BC17\] is

\(\|Tz-z_\star\|_G^2\le\|z-z_\star\|_G^2-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|Tz-z\|_G^2(z_\star\in\mathrm{Fix}T).\)

Taking a _G_-nearest fixed point and using norm equivalence with the error bound gives \(\mathrm{dist}_G(Tz,\mathrm{Fix}T)^2\le\rho^2\mathrm{dist}_G(z,\mathrm{Fix}T)^2\) whenever \(\mathrm{dist}(z,\mathrm{Fix}T)\le t_0\). The initial condition gives \(\mathrm{dist}_G(z^0,\mathrm{Fix}T)\le\sqrt{g_\mathrm{min}}t_0\), and Fejér monotonicity preserves it, so \(\mathrm{dist}(z^k,\mathrm{Fix}T)\le t_0\) for every _k_; this proves (F.1) and its Euclidean form. Nonexpansiveness gives \(\|Tz-z\|_G\le 2\mathrm{dist}_G(z,\mathrm{Fix}T)\), so the step lengths have a geometrically summable tail and the iterates converge R-linearly to some point of Fix_T_. For an arbitrary starting point, averagedness gives boundedness and square summability of \(\|Tz^k-z^k\|_G\). A cluster point is fixed by continuity. Fejér monotonicity relative to it gives convergence of the whole sequence, which therefore eventually enters the neighborhood above.

Q-linear contraction is asserted in the _G_ metric; norm equivalence yields R-linear distance and iterate bounds in the original coordinates, not necessarily one-step contraction in every equivalent norm.

## F.2 ADMM and exact sGS-ADMM share one shadow map

The shared shadow representation of this subsection was established in the afterimage paper \[KY26a,  1 and Appendix A.2\]; we spell it out in the present notation, since the error-bound transfer of §5 acts on it. Note that for \(\tau\neq 1\) the map \(T_{\sigma,\tau}\) is _not_ the scalar relaxation \((1-\tau)\mathrm{Id}+\tau T_{\sigma,1}\); the multiplier step rescales the two orthogonal residual components blockwise. For \(\sigma>0\) and \(0<\tau<2\), exact ADMM on the dual SDP (3.1) is

\(\lambda^{k+1}=(\mathcal{A}\mathcal{A}^*)^{-1}\big[\sigma^{-1}b-\mathcal{A}(\sigma^{-1}X^k+S^k-C)\big],\) (F.2)

\(S^{k+1}=\Pi_+\big(C-\mathcal{A}^*\lambda^{k+1}-\sigma^{-1}X^k\big),\) (F.3)

\(X^{k+1}=X^k+\tau\sigma(\mathcal{A}^*\lambda^{k+1}+S^{k+1}-C).\) (F.4)

Define the shadow \(Z^k:=\mathsf{P}^\perp X^k+X_b-\sigma\mathsf{P}S^k-\sigma\mathsf{P}^\perp C\). Substitution in the first two equations gives

\(S^{k+1}=-\sigma^{-1}\Pi_-(Z^k),\) (F.5)

because \(\sigma(C-\mathcal{A}^*\lambda^{k+1})-X^k=-Z^k\) (check the R and N components separately using (F.2)); and the multiplier update reduces to the filter

\(X^{k+1}=(1-\tau)X^k+\tau\Pi_+(Z^k).\) (F.6)

Projecting the next shadow onto R and N then yields \(\mathsf{P}Z^{k+1}=\mathsf{P}Z^k-r^\|(Z^k)\) and \(\mathsf{P}^\perp Z^{k+1}=\mathsf{P}^\perp Z^k-\tau r_\sigma^\perp(Z^k)\), which is the shadow recursion \(T_{\sigma,\tau}\) of §5.

The exact sGS variant \[CST17\] inserts a second equality solve: \(\lambda^{k+1/2}\) by (F.2), then _S_<sup>_k_+1</sup> by (F.3) with \(\lambda^{k+1/2}\), then \(\lambda^{k+1}\) by (F.2) with _S_<sup>_k_+1</sup>, then (F.4). The same shadow gives (F.5), while the last two equations give

\(X^{k+1}=(\mathrm{Id}-\tau\mathsf{P})X^k+\tau X_b+\tau\sigma\mathsf{P}^\perp(S^{k+1}-C),\) (F.7)

whose N projection again yields \(\mathsf{P}^\perp Z^{k+1}=\mathsf{P}^\perp Z^k-\tau r_\sigma^\perp(Z^k)\); the R projection of the shadow depends only on _S_<sup>_k_+1</sup> and matches ADMM. Thus both algorithms share the recursion \(T_{\sigma,\tau}\); the shadow records only the pair \((\mathsf{P}^\perp X^k,\mathsf{P}S^k)\), not all of (_X<sup>k</sup>,S<sup>k</sup>_).

## F.3 Parameter-dependent metric and rates for the shadow map

**Proposition F.2** (A parameter-dependent metric for the shadow map)**.** _For_ \(0<\tau<2\), \(T_{\sigma,\tau}\) _is_ \(\alpha_\tau\)_-averaged with_ \(\alpha_\tau=\mathrm{max}\{1,\tau\}/2\) _in the metric_ \(\mathsf{G}_\tau:=\mathsf{P}+\tau^{-1}\mathsf{P}^\perp\)_, whose eigenvalues bound it between_ \(\mathrm{min}\{1,\tau^{-1}\}\) _and_ \(\mathrm{max}\{1,\tau^{-1}\}\) _times the Frobenius metric._

_Proof of Theorem F.2._ Write \(T_{\sigma,\tau}=\mathrm{Id}-\mathsf{D}_\tau R_0\) with \(R_0:=\mathrm{Id}-T_{\sigma,1}\), which is firmly nonexpansive because the canonical DR map is \[BC17\]. Put _e=Z-W_ and _v=R_<sub>0</sub>_Z-R_<sub>0</sub>_W_, so \(\langle e,v\rangle\ge\|v\|_F^2\). With \(\mathsf{G}_\tau=\mathsf{D}_\tau^{-1}\), self-adjointness gives

\(\|e-\mathsf{D}_\tau v\|_{\mathsf{G}_\tau}^2=\|e\|_{\mathsf{G}_\tau}^2-2\langle e,v\rangle+\langle v,\mathsf{D}_\tau v\rangle\le\|e\|_{\mathsf{G}_\tau}^2-\big(\frac{2}{\mathrm{max}\{1,\tau\}}-1\big)\|\mathsf{D}_\tau v\|_{\mathsf{G}_\tau}^2,\)

using \(\langle v,\mathsf{D}_\tau v\rangle\le\mathrm{max}\{1,\tau\}\|v\|_F^2\le\mathrm{max}\{1,\tau\}\langle e,v\rangle\). This is the averagedness inequality with \(\alpha_\tau=\mathrm{max}\{1,\tau\}/2<1\) for \(\tau<2\); the metric bounds are the two eigenvalues of \(\mathsf{G}_\tau\).

_Proof of Theorem 5.1._ Combine (5.1), Theorem F.2, and Theorem F.1: the shadow distance contracts eventually Q-linearly in \(\mathsf{G}_\tau\) and the shadow converges R-linearly to some \(\bar{Z}=\bar{X}-\sigma\bar{S}\in\mathcal{Z}_\star\) (in the Boolean case \(\bar{X}=X_\star\)). For the raw variables: projections are Lipschitz, so \(\Pi_+(Z^k)\rightarrow\bar{X}\) and \(S^{k+1}\rightarrow\bar{S}\) R-linearly by (F.5). For ADMM, (F.6) is a stable linear recurrence with factor \(|1-\tau|<1\). Hence \(X^k\rightarrow\bar{X}\) R-linearly at any rate \(\widehat{\rho}\in(\mathrm{max}\{\rho,|1-\tau|\},1)\); the enlargement also absorbs the \(k\rho^k\) term when the two rates coincide. Then (F.2) transfers R-linear convergence to \(\lambda^{k+1}\), whose limit is the unique multiplier of \(\bar{S}\). For sGS-ADMM, (F.7) gives the exact contraction \(\mathsf{P}X^{k+1}-X_b=(1-\tau)(\mathsf{P}X^k-X_b)\). The component \(\mathsf{P}^\perp X^k=\mathsf{P}^\perp Z^k+\sigma\mathsf{P}^\perp C\) is read off the shadow. Together with the equality-solve formulas, this proves R-linear convergence of all raw sequences.

**Proposition F.4** (PDHG parameter-dependent metric)**.** _If_ \(\theta:=\sqrt{\eta_x\eta_y}\|\mathcal{A}\|_\mathrm{op}<1\)_, then T_<sub>P</sub> _is firmly nonexpansive in_ \(\mathsf{G}_\mathrm{P}:=\left[\begin{array}{ c c }
