Direct substitution from the PDHG update gives \(0\in\mathsf{F}_\mathrm{KKT}(w^+)+\mathsf{G}_\mathrm{P}(w^+-w)\), the preconditioned proximal-point form of PDHG \[CP11, OV20\]; monotonicity applied to two such inclusions gives \(\|w^+-\bar{w}^+\|_{\mathsf{G}_\mathrm{P}}^2\le\langle w^+-\bar{w}^+,w-\bar{w}\rangle_{\mathsf{G}_\mathrm{P}}\), which is firm nonexpansiveness.

_Proof of Theorem 5.2._ Apply Theorem F.1 with \(\alpha=1/2\), Theorems F.3 and F.4. R-linear convergence of the slack follows from \(S^k=C-\mathcal{A}^*\lambda^k\) and Lipschitz continuity.

## G Genericity

Two clarifications on scope. First, genericity is asserted in the full coefficient space P_<sub>n</sub>_; a structured subfamily (sparse, low-degree, or symmetric) is measure-zero and needs its own relative-genericity argument. Second, full row rank of A_<sub>d</sub>_ is a representation choice made once and for all in Theorem B.1, not a property supplied by genericity. Under an arbitrary split in (6.1), the vectors _w<sub>A</sub>_ can be linearly dependent, and the kernel of _S_<sub>int</sub> can be strictly larger than span{_u_}. The convention stated in §6 is what makes them a basis of \(u^\perp\).

## G.1 Full order: proof of Theorem 6.1

_Proof of Theorem 6.1._ Define the point indicators \(\ell_a(x):=2^{-n}\prod_{i=1}^n(1+a_ix_i)=2^{-n}\sum_{T\subseteq[n]}a^Tx^T\). Modulo _I_<sub>B</sub>, \(\ell_a^2\equiv\ell_a\) and \(\sum_a\ell_a\equiv 1\). At full order the moment PSD condition tests the square of every Boolean function, so \(\pi_a:=L_y(\ell_a)=L_y(\ell_a^2)\ge 0\) and \(\sum_a\pi_a=1\); the interpolation identity \(h\equiv\sum_ah(a)\ell_a\) gives \(L_y(h)=\sum_a\pi_ah(a)\), i.e. the simplex representation. The vectors _b<sub>n</sub>(a_) are mutually orthogonal because \(b_n(a)^\top b_n(b)=\prod_i(1+a_ib_i)=2^n\mathbf{1}_{\{a=b\}}\), which proves uniqueness of the coefficients and, for uniquely minimized _f_, uniqueness of the optimizer \(b_n(x_\star)b_n(x_\star)^\top\).

For upward persistence, let _d_<sub>0</sub> be an order at which _f_ is uniquely rank-one exact and let \(d_0<d\le n\). An order-_d_ optimizer truncates to an order-_d_<sub>0</sub> feasible matrix with the same objective value, since \(\mathrm{deg}f\le 2d_0\). Hierarchy monotonicity and the feasible lift of _x<sub>⋆</sub>_ give \(p_{d_0}(f)\le p_d(f)\le f(x_\star)=p_{d_0}(f)\). So the truncation is the unique lower-order optimum; in particular _y_<sub>{_i_}</sub>=_x<sub>⋆,i</sub>_ for all _i_. Choose Gram vectors _g<sub>A</sub>_ of the higher-order optimizer with \(\langle g_A,g_B\rangle=y_{A\triangle B}\) and \(\|g_A\|=1\). Whenever \(A,A\triangle\{i\}\in\mathcal{I}_d\), \(\langle g_A,g_{A\triangle\{i\}}\rangle=x_{\star,i}\in\{\pm 1\}\), so equality in Cauchy-Schwarz gives \(g_{A\triangle\{i\}}=x_{\star,i}g_A\). Adding the elements of _A_ one at a time gives \(g_A=x_\star^Ag_\emptyset\). Hence the optimizer is \(b_d(x_\star)b_d(x_\star)^\top\).

For the certificate: with _g_:=_f-f(x<sub>⋆</sub>_) and _c<sub>a</sub>_:=2<sup>-_n_</sup>_b<sub>n</sub>(a_), set

\(S_\mathrm{full}:=\sum_{a\neq x_\star} g(a)c_ac_a^\top.\) (G.1)

One has \(b_n(x)^\top c_ac_a^\top b_n(x)\equiv\ell_a(x)^2\), so _S_<sub>full</sub> represents \(\sum_{a\neq x_\star} g(a)\ell_a^2\equiv\sum_ag(a)\ell_a\equiv g\); all displayed weights _g(a_) are positive by unique minimality, and orthogonality of the _b<sub>n</sub>(a_) gives ker(_S_<sub>full</sub>)=span{_b<sub>n</sub>(x<sub>⋆</sub>_)}.

## G.2 Fixed-order cells: proof of Theorem 6.2

Recall the cells of §6: for _u=b<sub>d</sub>(a_),

\(\mathcal{Q}(a,d):=\{g\in\mathcal{P}_{\le 2d}:g(a)=0\},\mathcal{E}(a,d):=\big\{g\in\mathcal{Q}(a,d):\mathrm{argmin}_{X\in\mathcal{X}_d}\langle C_g,X\rangle=\{uu^\top\}\big\},\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d):=\{g\in\mathcal{Q}(a,d):\exists S\unknown 0,\mathcal{G}_d(S)=g,\mathrm{ker}(S)=\mathrm{span}\{u\}\}.\text{(G.2)}\)

Suppose a certificate _S_ of E<sub>sc</sub>(_a,d_) exists. Every feasible _X_ has value \(\langle S,X\rangle\ge 0\), while \(uu^\top\) has value zero. Equality forces \(\mathrm{ran}(X)\subseteq\mathrm{ker}(S)=\mathrm{span}\{u\}\), and \(X_{\emptyset,\emptyset}=1\) then gives \(X=uu^\top\). Hence \(\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d)\subseteq\mathcal{E}(a,d)\). In particular, the definition of E<sub>sc</sub>(_a,d_) may ask only that some PSD Gram matrix with kernel span{_u_} represents _g_; optimality is automatic.

The family (6.1) gives a linear right inverse of G_<sub>d</sub>_ on Q(_a,d_). Each \(w_\Gamma\) satisfies \(w_\Gamma^\top u=0\) and \(\mathcal{G}_d(w_\Gamma w_\Gamma^\top)=\psi_\Gamma:=2(1-a^\Gamma x^\Gamma)\). The |I<sub>2_d_</sub>|-1 polynomials \(\psi_\Gamma\) form a basis of Q(_a,d_). Define the section \(\mathscr{B}_{a,d}(\sum_\Gamma t_\Gamma\psi_\Gamma):=\sum_\Gamma t_\Gamma w_\Gamma w_\Gamma^\top\). It obeys G_<sub>d</sub>_(B<sub>_a,d_</sub>(_h_))=_h_ and B<sub>_a,d_</sub>(_h)u_=0. Since \(t_\Gamma=-a^\Gamma h_\Gamma/2\) and \(\|w_\Gamma w_\Gamma^\top\|_\mathrm{op}=2\),

\(\|\mathscr{B}_{a,d}(h)\|_\mathrm{op}\le\sum_{\Gamma\neq\emptyset}|h_\Gamma|\le\sqrt{|\mathcal{I}_{2d}|-1}\|h\|_\mathrm{coef},\) (G.3)

where \(\|h\|_\mathrm{coef}\) is the Euclidean norm of the coefficient vector. By the split convention of §6, \(w_A=e_A-a^Ae_\emptyset\), and these _N_-1 vectors are orthogonal to _u_ and linearly independent. Hence the interior certificate _S_<sub>int</sub> of (6.1) satisfies \(S_\mathrm{int}\unknown 0\), ker(_S_<sub>int</sub>)=span{_u_}, and G_<sub>d</sub>(S_<sub>int</sub>)=_r<sub>a,d</sub>_:=2\(\sum_{\emptyset\neq A\in\mathcal{I}_d}(1-a^Ax^A)\). In particular \(r_{a,d}\in\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d)\), so the cell is nonempty.

_Proof of Theorem 6.2. Openness._ Fix \(g\in\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d)\), and let _S_ be a certificate for _g_ that is positive definite on \(u^\perp\). Write \(\kappa>0\) for the smallest eigenvalue of _S_ restricted to \(u^\perp\). For \(h\in\mathcal{Q}(a,d)\), the matrix _S_+B_<sub>a,d</sub>(h_) still annihilates _u_ and represents _g+h_. By (G.3) it stays positive definite on \(u^\perp\) whenever \(\|h\|_\mathrm{coef}<\kappa/(2\sqrt{|\mathcal{I}_{2d}|-1})\). Hence \(g+h\in\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d)\).

_Density._ If \(g\in\mathcal{E}(a,d)\), primal Slater gives an optimal Gram matrix \(S\unknown 0\) representing _g_, and \(u^\top Su=g(a)=0\) forces _Su_=0. For every \(\varepsilon>0\), \(S+\varepsilon S_\mathrm{int}\) represents \(g+\varepsilon r_{a,d}\) and is positive definite on \(u^\perp\), so \(g+\varepsilon r_{a,d}\in\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}(a,d)\), and \(g+\varepsilon r_{a,d}\rightarrow g\) as \(\varepsilon\rightarrow 0\).

_Semialgebraicity._ With \(P_{u^\perp}=I_N-uu^\top/N\), membership in E<sub>sc</sub>(_a,d_) is the existential first-order formula \(\exists S,t:\mathcal{G}_d(S)=g,Su=0,S-tP_{u^\perp}\unknown 0\), _t\>_0; PSD-ness is finitely many minor inequalities. Membership in E(_a,d_) is \(g\in\mathcal{Q}(a,d)\) together with \(\nexists X\in\mathcal{X}_d:\|X-uu^\top\|_F^2>0,\langle C_g,X\rangle\le 0\). The Tarski-Seidenberg theorem and closure under complements make both cells semialgebraic \[BCR98\].

_Dimension._ Abbreviate E<sub>sc</sub>:=E<sub>sc</sub>(_a,d_) and E:=E(_a,d_); density gives \(\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}\subseteq\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathrm{cl}\mathcal{E}_\mathrm{sc}\). The semialgebraic frontier theorem gives dim(clE<sub>sc</sub>\\E<sub>sc</sub>)_\<_dimE<sub>sc</sub> and dimclE<sub>sc</sub>=dimE<sub>sc</sub> \[BCR98, Propositions 2.8.2 and 2.8.13\]. Hence dim(E\\E<sub>sc</sub>)_\<_dimE. The open neighborhood of _r<sub>a,d</sub>_ shows dimE=dimQ(_a,d_)=|I<sub>2_d_</sub>|-1. The exceptional set therefore has zero Lebesgue measure in Q(_a,d_).

### G.3 Ambient genericity

**Proposition G.1** (Simultaneous SC at every uniquely rank-one exact order)**.** _There is an open dense full-measure semialgebraic set_ \(\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{gen}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_n\) _such that every_ \(f\in\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{gen}\) _has a unique Boolean minimizer and, at every order_ \(d_\star(f)\le d\le n\)_, the relaxation admits a rank-(N<sub>d</sub>_-1) _optimal certificate._

_Proof._ First exclude the finite union of proper tie hyperplanes \(E_\mathrm{tie}:=\bigcup_{a\neq b}\{f:f(a)=f(b)\}\); each is proper because some linear monomial distinguishes _a_ from _b_. For each pair (_a,d_), let _B<sub>a,d</sub>_:=E(_a,d_)\\E<sub>sc</sub>(_a,d_) and lift it to the full coefficient space by the additive constant, \(\widetilde{B}_{a,d}:=\{g+c:g\in B_{a,d},c\in\mathbb{R}\}\). The map \((g,c)\mapsto g+c\) is injective on this domain (because _g(a_)=0 recovers _c=f(a_)), so for nonempty _B<sub>a,d</sub>_,

\(\mathrm{dim}\widetilde{B}_{a,d}=\mathrm{dim}B_{a,d}+1<|\mathcal{I}_{2d}|\le 2^n\)

by Theorem 6.2. Let _E_<sub>bad</sub> be the union of _E_<sub>tie</sub> with the finitely many \(\widetilde{B}_{a,d}\), and set G<sub>gen</sub>:=P_<sub>n</sub>_\\cl_E_<sub>bad</sub>. Finite unions and closures preserve semialgebraicity and dimension, so dimcl_E_<sub>bad</sub>_\<_2_<sup>n</sup>_ and G<sub>gen</sub> is open, dense, and full measure. For \(f\in\mathcal{G}_\mathrm{gen}\) with minimizer _x<sub>⋆</sub>_, Theorem 6.1 gives \(d_\star(f)\le n\) and unique rank-one exactness at every order \(d\in[d_\star(f),n]\). At each such order, \(f-f(x_\star)\in\mathcal{E}(x_\star,d)\). Since _f_ avoids the corresponding lifted bad set, this normalized objective lies in E<sub>sc</sub>(_x<sub>⋆</sub>,d_).

The proof of Theorem 6.3 in §6 assembles Theorem G.1 with Theorems B.1, B.2, 3.2 and 4.2 and the transfer results of §5.

## H Details of the Illustrative Experiments

This appendix records the setup behind Figure 1 and one further illustration for a higher-degree objective. The experiments are illustrations of the theory rather than a benchmark; no timing comparison is intended.

### General setup.

All runs except the saved run of panel (a) use the exact ADMM of §5 with multiplier step \(\tau=1\) and a fixed penalty \(\sigma\) (reported per experiment), implemented in MATLAB, stopped when the maximal KKT residual falls below 10<sup>-10</sup>. The maximal KKT residual is max{_r_<sub>p</sub>_,r_<sub>d</sub>_,r_<sub>g</sub>} with _r_<sub>p</sub>=<tbc>

\(\|\mathcal{A}X-b\|_2/(1+\|b\|_2)\), \(r_\mathrm{d}=\|\mathcal{A}^*\lambda+S-C\|_F/(1+\|C\|_F)\), and \(r_\mathrm{g}=|\langle C,X\rangle-b^\top\lambda|/(1+|\langle C,X\rangle|+|b^\top\lambda|)\). Symmetric matrices are vectorized by the orthonormal svec, with off-diagonal entries scaled by \(\sqrt{2}\), so Euclidean distances in these coordinates equal Frobenius distances. Panels (a) and (c) of each figure report the fixed-point residual \(\|Z^{k+1}-Z^k\|_F\) of the shadow sequence of §5 on a logarithmic scale. Unique rank-one exactness and the existence of a strictly complementary certificate are verified once per instance. We solve both sides of the relaxation with an interior-point solver at tolerance 10<sup>-14</sup> and inspect the spectra of the optimal pair. Throughout, "certified" means that the Boolean minimum and its uniqueness are established by exhaustive enumeration of all 2_<sup>n</sup>_ cube points (exact up to floating-point summation); rank and strict-complementarity statements are numerical, at the stated tolerances. All rank readouts in this appendix use a 10<sup>-6</sup> relative eigenvalue tolerance. All new runs were performed on a laptop with an Apple M2 Max processor and 64GB of RAM.

## Instances.

_BQP-20_: the binary quadratic instance BQP-r1-20-1 of \[KJY25\], with _n_=20 and standard Gaussian _Q_ and _c_; Figure 1(a) is that paper’s saved run on the standard (non-quotient) second-order relaxation, with _N_=231, _m_=20,601, and \(\sigma=100\). _BQP-20q_: an independent Gaussian instance with _n_=20, used for Figure 1(b)-(c) on the quotient relaxation of §2 (_N_=211, _m_=16,171, \(\sigma=1\)). It is certified by direct enumeration of the 2<sup>20</sup> cube points and an interior-point solve. The minimizer is unique, with the second-smallest cube value 0.69 above the minimum; the relaxation value matches the minimum to relative error below 10<sup>-13</sup>; and a strictly complementary certificate of rank _N_-1=210 exists. _PBO4-20_: a dense degree-\(\le 4\) Boolean objective with standard Gaussian coefficients and _n_=20, relaxed at order _d_=2 (_N_=211, _m_=16,171, \(\sigma=1\)). It is certified like BQP-20q, with the cube scan performed by a fast Walsh-Hadamard transform. The minimizer is unique, with the second-smallest cube value 15.6 above the minimum; the relaxation value matches the minimum to relative error below 10<sup>-13</sup>; and a strictly complementary certificate of rank 210 exists. Not every Gaussian quartic is order-two exact: the first sampled seed has relative relaxation gap \(7.8\times 10^{-2}\), and the certified instance is the second seed.

## Cold start (Figure 1(a)).

The run converges in 4,583 iterations. The limiting primal iterate has numerical rank one, identified at iteration 1,113 (the dotted line in Figure 1(a)). The limiting certificate has numerical rank 210 out of _N_-1=230, with \(\lambda_\mathrm{min}(X_\mathrm{lim}+\sigma S_\mathrm{lim})\approx 4\times 10^{-15}\). So the limiting pair is not strictly complementary. The sharp linear phase begins essentially at rank identification.

## Sampling singular endpoints (Figure 1(b)).

For fixed \(\sigma\), the fixed points of the shadow recursion are \(\mathcal{Z}_\star=\{X_\star-\sigma S:S\in\mathcal{S}_\star\}\) (§3), so sampling an endpoint means sampling an optimal certificate. We draw a symmetrized standard Gaussian matrix _R_ and minimize \(\langle R,S\rangle\) over the optimal certificate slice \(\mathcal{S}_\star=(S_\mathrm{sc}+\mathcal{L})\cap\mathbb{S}_+(V)\) with an interior-point solver. For a generic _R_ the minimizer is unique and is an extreme point of S_<sub>⋆</sub>_. Extreme points of the positive-dimensional set S_<sub>⋆</sub>_ lie on its relative boundary, where certificates lose rank. One hundred independent draws on BQP-20q give certificates _S<sub>i</sub>_ of numerical rank 68 to 72 (median 69), against the strictly complementary rank _N_-1=210. The corresponding endpoints \(\bar{Z}_i=X_\star-\sigma S_i\) have numerical ranks 68 to 72 (median 70), far below the full rank _N_=211 attained at the strictly complementary endpoint; Figure 1(b) plots their distribution. Both readouts are relative to the matrix’s own largest eigenvalue; since \(\|\bar{Z}_i\|_\mathrm{op}\approx N\) while \(\|S_i\|_\mathrm{op}\) is much smaller, the numerical rank of \(\bar{Z}_i\) need not equal 1+rank(_S<sub>i</sub>_). The endpoints are also essentially different from one another: the pairwise distances \(\|\bar{Z}_i-\bar{Z}_j\|_F=\sigma\|S_i-S_j\|_F\) lie in \[15.7,16.7\], comparable to the certificate norms \(\|S_i\|_F\approx 13\) themselves.

## Near-singular warm starts (Figure 1(c)).

The _i_-th run starts at \(Z_i^0=\bar{Z}_i+\varepsilon G_i\) with \(\varepsilon=10^{-3}\), where _G<sub>i</sub>_ has independent standard Gaussian entries in the svec coordinates. The perturbation has norm about \(\varepsilon\sqrt{N(N+1)/2}\approx 0.15\), below \(10^{-3}\|\bar{Z}_i\|_F\). So every start lies near a singular endpoint rather than at it. All 100 runs converge. The iteration counts lie in \[4,008, 5,124\] (median 4,922). Each limiting moment iterate has rank one, and each limiting certificate stays within 0.11 in Frobenius norm (about one percent of its size) of its sampled certificate _S<sub>i</sub>_. At the stated tolerance these limiting certificates have numerical rank 210, so the iteration stops at nonsingular endpoints close to the singular samples.
